hints: Start at the very beginning of one heartbeat. Where does the wave of excitation always start, and what must the atria do immediately after?
Remember why there must be a short pause at the AVN before the ventricles contract, and what carries the impulse down the septum to the base of the ventricles.
walkthrough:
**Start at the pacemaker**

The cardiac cycle is initiated by the sinoatrial node (SAN). So the first event must be X: wave of excitation spreads from the sinoatrial node.

This wave spreads across the atrial walls, so the next event is T: atrial walls contract, pushing blood into the ventricles.

**Pause to let ventricles fill**

The excitation then reaches V: wave enters the atrioventricular node (AVN). Here it is U: delayed by a fraction of a second.

This delay is vital. It ensures the atria have finished contracting and the ventricles are full before they contract.

**Ventricular contraction**

After the delay, the impulse travels rapidly W: down the bundle of His and Purkyne tissue to the base of the ventricles. This causes Y: ventricles contract, from the base upwards.

So the full logical order is: X -> T -> V -> U -> W -> Y -> back to X. Only diagram C shows this loop.

options.A: Starts at V (AVN) and puts ventricular contraction Y before atrial contraction T, which is backwards. Atria must contract first.
options.B: Puts the delay U before the impulse even reaches the AVN V, and puts Purkyne conduction W after ventricular contraction Y. Both are the wrong way round.
options.C: Shows the correct loop: X (SAN fires) -> T (atria contract) -> V (to AVN) -> U (delay) -> W (Purkyne) -> Y (ventricles contract).
options.D: Puts atrial contraction T after the AVN V and before the delay U, and puts Purkyne conduction W after ventricular contraction Y. The order is mixed up.
